short: An artificial harbour built north of Ostia because the Tiber's mouth silted too fast to serve Rome's grain fleet.
full:
Claudius began building a large artificial harbour, Portus, about three kilometres north of Ostia in 42 CE, after storms repeatedly wrecked ships anchored off the silt-choked river mouth that had served Rome for centuries. Two curved moles enclosed a basin of some 150 hectares, marked at its entrance by a lighthouse modelled on the Pharos of Alexandria and built, according to Pliny, on the hull of the ship that had brought an obelisk from Egypt to Rome. Trajan added an inner hexagonal basin of about 33 hectares, completed by 112 CE, giving ships sheltered berths and greatly increasing capacity for handling grain shipments.

A canal, the Fossa Traiana, linked the new basin to the Tiber, allowing barges to move grain and other cargo upriver to Rome without transferring it at Ostia. Portus effectively replaced Ostia as Rome's main harbour and remained central to feeding the city until the western empire's collapse; silting and the retreat of the coastline eventually stranded the site inland, and the hexagonal basin, still traceable today, survives largely intact as one of the clearest surviving examples of Roman harbour engineering.
